questions.q: Saving the return address in a single register (such as R15) works for a single function call that makes no nested calls.
questions.explain: With one call, R15 holds the address of the next instruction, the function jumps back to it, and execution continues normally. It only breaks once a called function calls another function.

questions.q: Using only R15 to hold return addresses, _start calls print_hello and print_hello calls print_goodbye. print_goodbye returns correctly. What happens when print_hello then tries to return through R15?
choices: It returns correctly to _start and the program exits
It jumps to print_goodbye again and prints "goodbye!" forever
It jumps back to its own return instruction again and again, an infinite loop
The CPU automatically restores the earlier value of R15
questions.explain: The nested call overwrote R15 with print_hello's own resume address. So print_hello's return jumps to itself, reads the same R15, and jumps to itself again forever.

questions.q: What is the root cause of the single-register scheme failing on nested calls?
choices: A register cannot hold a 64-bit address
Only one return address can be stored, so a nested call overwrites the caller's saved address
The kernel clears R15 during every syscall
jmp can only jump forward in memory
questions.explain: One register is room for exactly one address. What is needed is a place to store as many return addresses as there are nested calls, without overwriting any of them.

questions.q: What was the call stack originally created to do? (Other features were added to it later.)
choices: Store return addresses so nested function calls can each find their way back
Store the string data a program prints
Store syscall numbers for the kernel
Hold only local variables
questions.explain: At its core the call stack is a list of slots for return addresses. Storing local variables and other uses came later.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: On a 64-bit system, how many bytes does each saved return address take up?
questions.explain: A 64-bit address is 8 bytes (a quadword), so each stack slot is 8 bytes and the pointer moves by 8 per slot.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: To support 500 nested function calls, with each return address taking 8 bytes, how many bytes of stack space are needed (before rounding up)?
questions.explain: 500 x 8 = 4000 bytes. The lesson rounds this up to 4096 bytes (4 KB).

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: A hand-built call stack reserves 4096 bytes. How many 8-byte return-address slots fit in it?
questions.explain: 4096 / 8 = 512 slots, which is a bit more than the 500 nested calls the space was sized for.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: The space is reserved with `call_stack: .skip 4096, 0xFF`. What does the second operand (`0xFF`) do?
choices: It sets the alignment of the block to 0xFF bytes
It limits the stack to 0xFF slots
It marks the block as executable
It fills every reserved byte with 0xFF
questions.explain: Adding a comma and a value after the size sets every byte of the reserved space to that value. The lesson uses it to show the memory belongs to the program, then sets it back to zero.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: In the hand-built call stack, R15 is always left pointing at the next free slot, not at the most recently written one.
questions.explain: That is the rule the lesson follows: whoever saves an address next can write straight to [r15] without first adjusting the pointer.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: The return address is already in RAX. Which order of instructions saves it to the hand-built stack, following the 'write, then increment' rule?
choices: `add r15, 8` then `mov [r15], rax`
`mov [r15], rax` then `add r15, 8`
`sub r15, 8` then `mov [r15], rax`
`mov r15, rax` then `add r15, 8`
questions.explain: Write into the free slot R15 points at, then move R15 up 8 bytes to the next free slot.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: Which sequence correctly returns using the hand-built stack, following the 'decrement, then read' rule?
choices: `mov rax, [r15]`, `sub r15, 8`, `jmp rax`
`sub r15, 8`, `jmp r15`
`add r15, 8`, `mov rax, [r15]`, `jmp rax`
`sub r15, 8`, `mov rax, [r15]`, `jmp rax`
questions.explain: R15 points at the next free slot, so first back it up 8 bytes to the last saved address. Then load that address from memory into RAX and jump to it.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: Which instructions are part of the lesson's hand-built replacement for `call print_hello` (save the return address, then enter the function)?
choices: `lea rax, [resume_here]`
`mov [r15], rax`
`add r15, 8`
`jmp print_hello`
`sub r15, 8`
`mov rax, [r15]`
questions.explain: Load the resume address into RAX, write it to the slot R15 points at, move R15 to the next slot, then jump. The `sub r15, 8` and `mov rax, [r15]` instructions belong to the return sequence.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: R15 starts at 0x402000 (the start of call_stack). Two return addresses are saved, each with 'write, then add 8'. What is R15 now?
questions.explain: 0x402000 + 8 + 8 = 0x402000 + 16 = 0x402010 (16 decimal is 0x10 in hex). That is the third slot.

questions.category: Building a call stack by hand
questions.q: Continuing from R15 = 0x402010 with two addresses saved, print_goodbye returns once using 'decrement, then read'. What is R15 afterward?
questions.explain: Subtracting 8 from 0x402010 gives 0x402008, the second slot, which holds print_hello's resume address. That slot now counts as free again.

questions.q: What is the difference between `mov [r15], rax` and `mov r15, rax`?
choices: They do the same thing
`mov [r15], rax` writes RAX's value into memory at the address held in R15; `mov r15, rax` overwrites R15 itself
`mov [r15], rax` copies R15 into RAX
The brackets make the destination read-only
questions.explain: Brackets treat the register as a pointer: look at the address stored in R15 and go to that spot in memory. Without brackets, the register itself is the destination.

questions.q: After switching to the hand-built stack, print_goodbye still ends with `jmp r15`, and R15 = 0x402010. Why does this fail?
choices: It jumps to address 0x402010 itself, an empty data slot rather than code, so the program crashes
jmp cannot take a register as its operand
It jumps to the right return address, but one slot too early
It works correctly; nothing fails
questions.explain: Without brackets, jmp uses the value in R15 as the target. That value is the stack pointer (the free slot), not a saved return address, so execution lands in data and segfaults.

questions.q: `lea r15, [call_stack]` loads the address of the call_stack label into R15, not the bytes stored there.
questions.explain: lea (load effective address) computes the address. After it runs, R15 holds the starting address of the reserved block (0x402000 in the lesson).

questions.q: When the return address 0x40101D was written to a stack slot, its bytes looked reversed in the memory viewer. What is this byte-ordering format called?
choices: Big-endian
Two's complement
Little-endian
ASCII encoding
questions.explain: x86 stores multi-byte values little-endian, lowest byte first, so the address appears byte-reversed in memory.

questions.q: What does `call print_hello` do?
choices: Pushes the address of the instruction right after the call onto the stack
Jumps to print_hello
Saves the return address in R15
Pushes the address of the call instruction itself onto the stack
Pops the top value off the stack
questions.explain: call does two things in one instruction: it pushes the return address (the next instruction) onto the stack, then jumps to the target. This replaces the multi-line manual sequence.

questions.q: What does `ret` do?
choices: Pushes the current address onto the stack
Pops the address on top of the stack and jumps to it
Jumps to whatever address is in R15
Jumps back to the start of the program
questions.explain: ret is the reverse of call. It removes the return address from the top of the stack and continues execution there.

questions.q: _start contains `call print_hello` followed by `jmp exit`. Which address does `call print_hello` push onto the stack?
choices: The address of the `call print_hello` instruction
The address of the print_hello label
The address of the `jmp exit` instruction
The address of the exit label
questions.explain: The return address is always the instruction right after the call, so execution resumes at `jmp exit` when print_hello returns.

questions.q: print_hello ends with `call print_goodbye` followed by `ret`. Where does print_goodbye's own `ret` send execution?
choices: To the `jmp exit` instruction in _start
To the instruction right after `call print_goodbye`, the `ret` at the end of print_hello
To the first instruction of print_hello
Directly to the exit routine
questions.explain: print_goodbye returns to the instruction after its call, which is print_hello's ret. That ret then pops the next address and returns to `jmp exit` in _start.

questions.q: call and ret are built into the CPU hardware and are faster than doing the same work with several separate instructions by hand.
questions.explain: They provide the same function as the hand-built stack, but in single, hardwired instructions that also manage the stack pointer automatically.

questions.q: Which way does the CPU's built-in stack grow as values are pushed?
choices: From high memory addresses toward lower ones
From low memory addresses toward higher ones
It does not move; values overwrite one fixed slot
It alternates direction with each push
questions.explain: The real stack grows from high to low memory. Pushing subtracts from the stack pointer, the reverse of the hand-built stack, where R15 went up by 8 per save.

questions.q: When ret pops a return address, that slot in memory is zeroed out.
questions.explain: Nothing is cleared. The stack pointer just moves past the slot, so the old data is still in memory but no longer counts as part of the stack.

questions.q: One stack-terminology word: what does call do to the return address?
questions.explain: call pushes the return address onto the stack.

questions.q: One stack-terminology word: what does ret do to the return address?
questions.explain: ret pops the return address off the stack and jumps to it.

questions.q: What does `push rdx` do?
choices: Removes the top value of the stack and puts it in RDX
Sets RDX to zero
Jumps to the address held in RDX
Adds RDX's value onto the top of the stack
questions.explain: push places a register's value on the stack as a new top slot. RDX keeps its value.

questions.q: What does `pop rax` do?
choices: Copies RAX onto the top of the stack
Removes the top value from the stack and puts it in RAX
Clears the whole stack
Jumps to the address on top of the stack
questions.explain: pop takes the value off the top of the stack and loads it into the named register. That value then disappears from the visible stack.

questions.q: What value goes in RAX to request the exit system call?
questions.explain: `mov rax, 60` selects exit; `syscall` then runs it.

questions.q: What value goes in RAX to request the write system call used by print_hello?
questions.explain: `mov rax, 1` selects write. RDI = 1 sends output to the terminal.

questions.q: In print_hello's write syscall, which register holds the length of the string?
choices: RAX
RDI
RSI
RDX
questions.explain: RAX = syscall number (1, write), RDI = 1 (the terminal), RSI = address where the string starts, RDX = string length.

questions.q: Why does the exit routine run `xor rdi, rdi` before `syscall`?
choices: To pick the write syscall
It is an efficient way to set RDI to 0, which the kernel reports as the exit code
To flip every bit of RDI to 1
To pop the last return address off the stack
questions.explain: XORing a register with itself always gives 0. The kernel reads RDI as the exit code, so the program exits with code 0.
